newsitem.title: UK: UK to put jobs at top of its G7 agenda.
newsitem.headline: UK to put jobs at top of its G7 agenda.

text.p: Prime Minister Tony Blair will make his crusade for jobs and "employability" Britain's top priority at the annual summit of industrialised nations starting on Friday in Denver, Colorado.

British officials said Blair would tell his fellow leaders at the Group of Seven summit that they must grasp the nettle of globalisation by making their businesses flexible and their citizens adaptable to rapid economic change.

Seeking shelter from the changes blowing through the world economy is not an option, Blair -- swept to power in a landslide election victory on May 1 -- will say when he leads off the discussion on globalisation on Saturday afternoon.

Blair has already enlisted U.S. President Bill Clinton's support for a two-year G7 initiative to promote labour market flexibility with the aim of making concrete progress before next year's summit which the prime minister will host in Birmingham.
"It is a very good opportunity to get jobs, employability and economic reform right at the top of the agenda," a senior British official said before leaving for Denver.

Blair will tell the rest of the G7 that although their societies must be fair and cohesive, each of them must examine domestic employment regulations to ensure they are not hindering job creation and the way back into work for the unemployed.

His determination to put jobs at the top of the G7 agenda comes after Blair won support from European Union leaders at their Amsterdam summit earlier this week for a drive to boost jobs and create flexible labour markets.

Backed by Germany, Blair managed to frustrate a French demand for more EU money to be spent on jobs, arguing that modern economic realities meant training and education were more important than old-style state intervention and regulation.
Employability comes top of Blair's 10 point wish-list for the Denver summit. His other objectives are,
-- to ensure extra efforts to supervise international financial markets and combat financial fraud,
-- to get the G7 and Russia to take the lead on international environmental issues, including climate change,
-- to secure support for Britain's agenda on human rights, democracy and good government,
-- to make further progress towards an international ban on landmines,
-- to take further steps against international terrorism, organised crime and drug trafficking,
-- to focus the G7's aid efforts on the world's poorest countries, including the possibility of more debt reduction,
-- to make a further push to help developing countries by liberalising world trade and opening up rich-country markets to their exports,
-- to further promote the role of the United Nations in preventing conflict as well as encouraging institutional reform of the UN and an early resolution to its funding crisis, and,
-- to secure a clear message of support on Hong Kong to safeguard its civil liberties after the handover of the British colony to China on July 1.
As well as attending the main summit sessions, Blair has scheduled bilateral meetings with Clinton, Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
